blocks.text: 1. Data Pipelines
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504899-246379623.png

ML Pipelines, the previous topic, listed data ingestion and validation among its earliest stages. A Data Pipeline is the dedicated system responsible for moving and transforming data before it ever actually reaches an ML Pipeline in the first place.

It is distinct from the ML Pipeline itself, a Data Pipeline is specifically about getting clean, reliable data flowing at all, a genuinely necessary foundation the ML Pipeline then builds directly on top of. Bad data flowing in makes every downstream stage, no matter how carefully built, fundamentally unreliable, regardless of how sophisticated the model or pipeline logic sitting on top of it actually is.
2. Where Data Actually Comes From
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504900-47697589.png

In a real system, data genuinely comes from a variety of distinct sources. Application databases hold transaction records and user activity logs, the direct byproduct of a running product. Third-party APIs bring in external data from providers or partner systems entirely outside the organization's own infrastructure.

Event streams carry real-time clickstream data or sensor readings, arriving continuously rather than sitting statically in one place waiting to be queried. A Data Pipeline needs to handle this genuine variety of sources consistently, rather than treating each one as its own separate, ad hoc problem to solve independently.
3. Batch Versus Streaming Data Pipelines
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504900-860668652.png

This connects directly back to Batch Prediction and Real-Time Prediction, both covered in the Model Deployment module, the exact same underlying distinction now applied to data movement itself rather than to prediction serving. Batch data pipelines move large chunks of data together on a schedule, while streaming data pipelines move individual events continuously, as they actually happen.

Batch pipelines are simpler and genuinely sufficient for most reporting needs and periodic retraining requirements. Streaming pipelines are needed specifically when downstream systems require near-instant data freshness, feeding a real-time fraud detection model for instance, where waiting for the next scheduled batch would defeat the entire purpose.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline type","Best fit"],"rows":[["Batch","Periodic reporting and scheduled retraining, where latency is not critical"],["Streaming","Real-time features needing near-instant data freshness"]]}

blocks.text: 4. ETL Versus ELT
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504901-812224522.png

Extract, Transform, Load, commonly abbreviated ETL, transforms data before loading it into its final destination, meaning data arrives already cleaned and shaped, ready for immediate use the moment it lands. Extract, Load, Transform, or ELT, instead loads raw data first and transforms it later, only as actually needed.

ELT is generally more flexible, keeping the original raw data fully available for future, unforeseen needs that were not anticipated at the time the data was first ingested, an advantage worth genuinely weighing against ETL's more immediately usable, pre-shaped output depending on a given project's actual requirements.
5. Data Quality Checks at Entry
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504901-144355680.png

This connects back to the data health checks already introduced in the Monitoring topic. A Data Pipeline should validate data at the exact point it enters the system, not merely after it has already reached the model, catching problems as early and as cheaply as possible.

Schema checks confirm the expected columns and data types are actually present in incoming data. Range checks confirm values fall within a plausible, expected range, catching an obviously corrupted value before it propagates further. Completeness checks confirm a critical field is not missing far more often than genuinely expected, flagging a real upstream problem before it silently degrades everything downstream.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Catching a data quality problem at the pipeline's entry point is dramatically cheaper than discovering it only after it has already corrupted a trained model deployed to production. The earlier a check runs, the less damage a caught problem can actually do.

blocks.text: 6. Common Data Pipeline Failure Modes

An upstream schema change can silently break a downstream assumption, a column quietly renamed without any notice being the classic, recurring example. A source system going temporarily offline is another common failure mode, and the pipeline needs to handle that gap gracefully rather than crashing outright the moment it happens.

Duplicate records arriving from a retried, previously failed delivery attempt are a third common failure mode, requiring explicit deduplication logic built directly into the pipeline, since a naive pipeline will simply count the same event twice, quietly corrupting whatever downstream aggregation or model training relies on that data.

blocks.text: 7. Data Versioning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504902-802806157.png

This connects back to the data-version-tracking concern already raised in the ML Pipelines topic. A Data Pipeline should snapshot or version the data it produces at each stage, rather than simply overwriting the same location every single run with no record of what came before.

This versioning enables tracing a specific, already-trained model back to the exact data it was actually trained on, a genuinely essential capability whenever debugging an unexpected model behavior, or auditing exactly how a particular production model actually came to exist.
8. Matching Latency to Actual Need

A data pipeline feeding a nightly retraining job can genuinely tolerate hours of latency without causing any real problem, since the downstream consumer itself only runs once per day anyway. A data pipeline feeding a real-time fraud detection feature, by contrast, needs latency measured in seconds or less, since any meaningful delay directly undermines the entire purpose of catching fraud as it actually happens.

Matching a pipeline's actual latency to its downstream consumer's genuine need avoids over-engineering a low-latency streaming system where a much simpler batch pipeline would have worked perfectly well, and avoids under-engineering a pipeline that cannot keep pace with a genuinely latency-sensitive downstream requirement.
9. When a Dedicated Data Pipeline Matters Most

blocks.alt: When a Dedicated Data Pipeline Matters Most
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504902-88322520.png

A dedicated Data Pipeline matters most whenever data genuinely comes from multiple, distinctly different sources, consolidating and validating it consistently in one central place beats handling each source ad hoc, separately, within every individual project that happens to need it.

It matters just as much for any model that gets retrained regularly, which genuinely needs a reliable, repeatable data feed behind it, the direct data-side counterpart to the ML Pipeline automation already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A Data Pipeline moves and transforms data before it ever reaches an ML Pipeline, a necessary foundation.
Data comes from application databases, third-party APIs, and event streams, needing consistent, unified handling.
Batch data pipelines move large chunks on a schedule; streaming pipelines move individual events continuously.
ETL transforms data before loading; ELT loads raw data first and transforms it later, keeping raw data available.
Schema, range, and completeness checks at entry catch data quality problems as early and cheaply as possible.
Common failure modes: silent upstream schema changes, temporary source outages, and duplicate records.
Snapshotting or versioning data at each stage enables tracing a trained model back to its exact source data.
A pipeline's latency should match its downstream consumer's actual need, avoiding both over- and under-engineering.
Next up: Feature Stores, a centralized system for sharing computed features consistently across teams and pipelines.
